# Introduction

This chapter describes your completed senior thesis work,
including the overall aims and the background motivating your research. Whenever
possible, you should use one or more concrete examples and technical diagrams.

It is often useful and necessary to separate the introduction into multiple sections.
Several possible sections are proposed below, you can use these or distribute your
introductory text into sections in another way.

The headings below propose _one way_ you might structure this section of the document.

## Motivation

<!--
Explain the problem before you explain your solution. Two or three paragraphs is
usually enough when they answer: What is the problem? Who experiences it? Why
has it not been solved already? What are the consequences of leaving it unsolved?

Avoid openings such as "Computers are everywhere" or "In recent years,
technology has advanced rapidly." Specific beats generic: name the system, the
dataset, the practice, or the community you are writing about, and cite evidence
that the problem is real.
-->

## Current State of the Art

<!--
Summarize how the problem is handled today, by researchers and by practitioners.
You do not need to write the full literature review here; Chapter Two does that.
What you need here is enough context that a reader understands why your approach
is a reasonable next step.
-->

## Goals of the Project

<!--
State the goal so that it could be shown to be met or not met. "Improve software
testing" cannot be evaluated. "Reduce the false-positive reports of a mutation
testing tool on Java projects by 20% without losing real faults" can be.

Then list the objectives that support the goal, and keep them traceable:

  objective -> experiment in Chapter Four -> claim in Chapter Five

If an objective has no experiment, it is not an objective; it is an aspiration.
If a contribution has no objective behind it, you cannot defend it.
-->

## Scope and Assumptions

<!--
List the constraints you accept: the platforms you support, the languages your
tool targets, the size of the datasets you can handle, the users you assume.
Then list your assumptions and say what would break if each assumption failed.
Readers trust a thesis that names its limits more than one that claims none.
-->

## Key Terminology

<!--
Define the terms the rest of the thesis depends on. A definition list works well:

  **Mutation testing**: a technique that ... [@source]

Keep this section short. If a definition runs longer than three sentences, it
probably belongs in Chapter Two instead.

## Ethical Implications

This document requires that you discuss the ethical implications of your work -- no
matter how benign you consider the outcome of your project. As several major studies
of ethical issues in computer science assert: _no project is completely value-neutral_.

To assist you in elaborating on these issues, the following areas are topics you might
consider addressing. You do not need to address all of them.

* Information Privacy
* Information Accuracy (e.g., reliability)
* Potential Misuse (e.g., computer crime, unintended consequences)
* Second- or Third-Party Risk (e.g., safety)
* Data Collection Issues (e.g., issues inherent in collecting data)
* Algorithmic or Data Bias
* Potential Power Difference / Social Imbalance / Issues in Equity

In addition, reflect on ways that the above harms can be or are mitigated by your work.

<!--
Choose the two or three issues that genuinely apply to your project and discuss
them in a paragraph each. A short, specific discussion of two real harms is
stronger than a list that touches eight topics without committing to any of
them.

For each issue, answer: Who could be harmed? How would the harm occur? How
likely and how serious is it? What does your project do to reduce it, and what
remains unresolved? Chapter Five will ask you to revisit these questions.
-->
